disease_info: Major Depressive Disorder with Psychotic Features is characterized by a major depressive episode accompanied by hallucinations and/or delusions that are typically mood-congruent (e.g., themes of guilt, worthlessness, or deserved punishment). The psychotic features occur only during the depressive episode and do not persist independently, helping distinguish it from primary psychotic disorders such as schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder. Clinically, it often presents with pronounced functional impairment, high levels of distress, and an elevated risk of suicide, and may have a more severe and recurrent course than non-psychotic depression. Careful assessment of the temporal relationship between mood symptoms and psychosis, as well as exclusion of substance- or medical-induced causes, is crucial for accurate diagnosis and treatment planning.

narrative.personality: Shelly is a meticulous, routine-driven woman who finds comfort in orderly kitchen systems, quiet hobbies, and predictable days.
narrative.stressor: About six months before presentation, Shelly’s adult daughter abruptly moved several states away after a bitter argument about Shelly’s perceived controlling nature and her husband’s drinking, leaving Shelly feeling shut out and blamed. Around the same time, her husband cut back his hours due to back pain and began spending more evenings drinking in front of the TV, becoming emotionally distant and occasionally irritable, which disrupted the calm, structured home life she depended on. As the weeks went by, Shelly increasingly poured herself into work and church volunteering to avoid going home, but she began making uncharacteristic mistakes with inventory and missing her gardening club, which only reinforced her sense that she was “failing” as a wife, mother, and worker. After several months of this, she confided to her pastor that she had become preoccupied with the idea that her family would be better off without her, and at his urging and her supervisor’s concern about her declining performance, she agreed to see a psychiatrist.
narrative.chief_complaint: I keep thinking everyone would be better off if I just weren’t here anymore.

narrative.personality: Kip is a cautious, methodical retiree who channels his worry into careful planning, steady routines, and community involvement.
narrative.stressor: Roughly half a year before seeking help, Kip was diagnosed with congestive heart failure after a brief hospitalization for shortness of breath, which forced him to confront his mortality and scale back his cherished mentoring, gardening, and volunteer commitments. Used to feeling in control of risk and contingencies, he struggled with the unpredictability of his health, frequent medical appointments, and the loss of his previous stamina, leading him to decline invitations to serve on boards and to stop his regular hikes. As the months passed, he spent more time alone at home reviewing his finances and family genealogy, ruminating on whether he had truly provided for his children and what legacy he would leave, and he gradually withdrew from church and the food bank, which had previously anchored his weeks. His primary care physician became concerned when Kip mentioned that he was increasingly preoccupied with the idea that his life might already be effectively “over” and that he had started wondering whether it would be better to bring things to a close on his own terms, prompting an urgent psychiatric referral.
narrative.chief_complaint: Lately I keep thinking about how I might be better off dead and wondering if there’s any point in going on like this.

narrative.personality: Daniel is a laid-back, creative carpenter with a strong passion for woodwork and sustainable design but a tendency toward disorganization and drifting routines.
narrative.stressor: Four to five months before his evaluation, Daniel took on several large custom cabinetry projects at once, hoping to establish himself as an independent contractor, but he quickly became overwhelmed by the paperwork, deadlines, and client expectations due to his looser approach to scheduling. A couple of key jobs went badly—one client refused to pay in full after delays and another posted a harsh online review—leaving Daniel with unexpected debt, arguments with his landlord about late rent, and a growing sense that he was not cut out for the trade he loved. He responded by spending more time alone in his workshop and at home, letting calls go unanswered and skipping makerspace events and game nights, while his unfinished projects piled up and his confidence eroded. After a few months of this isolation and mounting pressure, he began experiencing vivid perceptions in the shop that frightened him and made it harder to work safely; when a friend noticed his increasing withdrawal and how unsettled he seemed and urged him to get help, Daniel agreed to see a psychiatrist.
narrative.chief_complaint: I’ve started seeing and hearing things in my workshop that I know shouldn’t be there, and it’s really freaking me out.
